anomaly_def.Name: Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Replication Synchronization Anomaly + Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Schema and Index Design Anomaly: Static mismatch between physical data model (table layout, indexes, partitioning, data types, constraints) and the workload’s access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths regardless of statistics freshness.
Replication Synchronization Anomaly: Replication pipeline cannot receive, persist, or apply WAL/redo at the rate generated by the primary, leading to widening log-position gaps and retention of log files.
Operating System Resource Limit Anomaly: Database or replication processes hit kernel-enforced ceilings for file handles, shared memory, semaphores, threads, I/O contexts, or cgroup quotas, causing allocation failures at the OS level.

When these three root causes strike concurrently, symptoms intertwine: 1) primary queries and background writers suffer high latency from full scans and non-covering index probes; 2) the heavier I/O and CPU load generated by those inefficient plans inflates the volume and velocity of transaction-log output; 3) replicas already starved for apply bandwidth fall further behind, exhibiting rapidly growing receive, write, flush, and replay lag; 4) as backlog accumulates, both primary and replica retain more WAL segments and relay files, increasing file-descriptor consumption and exacerbating kernel-level limits; 5) once per-process or cgroup caps for file handles, shared memory, or asynchronous I/O are exhausted, new client sessions, parallel workers, or replication threads fail to start, producing intermittent errors even for previously healthy operations; 6) monitoring shows simultaneous query slowdowns, replication delay spikes, and OS messages about ENFILE/EMFILE, out-of-shared-memory, or semaphore-allocation failures, making diagnosis difficult because each symptom can mask or mimic the others.

Causal chain: A poor schema/index design forces the engine to scan more pages and generate larger undo/redo records per transaction. The inflated WAL stream stresses the replication subsystem; apply threads on replicas must process more data per commit, which magnifies any existing network or CPU bottlenecks. As replicas lag, the primary is prevented from recycling old log segments, increasing on-disk log retention and the number of open file descriptors. The larger working-set and lingering logs require additional shared memory and kernel I/O contexts. Simultaneously, the extra CPU threads spawned for long-running queries and delayed replication apply workers drive process/thread counts upward. These cumulative pressures collide with conservative OS limits, causing resource-allocation failures that in turn throttle query execution and replication even further. The feedback loop—inefficient access paths → higher WAL volume → replication backlog → elevated kernel object usage → OS denials → further slowdown—creates a severe, multi-layer outage that is harder to resolve than any single anomaly alone.

entry.official_definition: The number of seconds to wait for more data from a source/replica connection before aborting the read.
entry.trigger_condition: A replica waits longer than replica_net_timeout for more data from the source connection.
entry.workload_impact: The replication network read is aborted and the replica considers the connection interrupted.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as a MySQL replication system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
